citation: Karat (no named authors). 'AI Workforce Transformation Report 2025-2026'. 8-page PDF (cover plus pages numbered 1-7), connect.karat.com, https://connect.karat.com/hubfs/2025-2026-AI-Workforce-Transformation-Report.pdf. Early highlights were posted 11.04.2025 at https://karat.com/resource/2025-ai-workforce-transformation-highlights/. Companion blog post: The Karat Team, 'Engineering interview trends 2026', karat.com, dated 01.07.2026, https://karat.com/engineering-interview-trends-2026/.
evidence_tier: Vendor survey. Karat sells interviewing-as-a-service, including an AI-enabled 'NextGen' interview product. Not peer-reviewed. No methodology appendix.
access_status: Fully read: the 2025-2026 PDF (downloaded, all text extracted; some charts are image-only, so the per-country bar values on pages 3 and 6 could not be read from the PDF text) and the karat.com 'Engineering interview trends 2026' post (read via fetch). Highlights page read. The 2026-2027 edition landing page (karat.com/resource/ai-workforce-transformation-report/) is a preview only. GeekWire, IT Brew and Business Wire coverage returned 403 and was not read.
sponsor_and_incentive: Karat funded and published the survey. Its business is technical interviewing, and the report's recommendation (human-led interviews where candidates may use AI) matches Karat's own product. The cohort comparison that favours 'Human + AI' interviews is the commercial point of the report. The Harris Poll is NOT named anywhere in the 2025-2026 PDF or the 2026 trends post. Harris Poll is credited for the separate 2026-2027 edition (157 technology leaders, U.S. and China), per City A.M., 8 October 2026 [uncertain: secondary press only].
exact_quotes: PDF p.1 (Executive Summary): "Key findings from our survey of 400 engineering leaders, including 300 SVPs and CXOs, across the U.S., India, and China reveal:"

PDF p.4: "The problem is, most organizations aren't yet assessing AI skills. 62% of leaders don't allow candidates to use AI in interviews. Just 30% of organizations ranked “updating technical assessments to assess for AI” as a top priority, and only 25% are prioritizing training interviewers. To make matters worse, leaders estimate that over half of candidates are using AI despite being instructed not to."
PDF p.5: "The signal from interviews that aren't AI-enabled is useless because most candidates are using AI."

PDF p.5: "But in the human + AI era, producing a working solution no longer generates the same hiring signal. Interviews must now isolate and independently measure a candidate's underlying skills while also assessing AI readiness."

PDF p.5: "As a result, the engineering leaders who aren't investing in next-generation assessments are getting less predictive hiring signals, and confidence in hiring is eroding, especially in the U.S."

PDF p.5 chart labels: "Increased difficulty assessing skills 2024 19% 2025 36% % US leaders who say it is difficult to accurately assess skills needed to capitalize on new developments in AI"; "Decreased hiring confidence 2024 67% 2025 47% % US leaders who are very confident that qualified candidates are the ones getting job offers"; "AI to blame 71% % leaders who say AI is making it harder to assess technical skills"

PDF p.6: "Human + AI: 33% of organizations in the U.S. use live interviews and allow candidates to use AI tools in a way that mirrors day-to-day work"; "Human-only: 45% of organizations in the U.S. measure technical skills using live interviews where AI use is prohibited"; "Non-human: 22% of organizations in the U.S. use a combination of online code tests and take home projects that do not include human interviewers"
PDF p.6: "The data shows organizations that allow candidates to use AI in human-led interviews anticipate stronger returns on their AI investments."
PDF p.6: "Chinese companies are almost twice as likely to allow the use of AI in interviews."
PDF p.2: "73% of leaders now say that a strong engineer is worth at least 3x their total compensation." and chart "59% Say weak engineers deliver net zero or negative value in the AI era"
PDF p.7: "These organizations are upgrading their interview content, rubrics, and interviewer training to assess not just problem-solving, but AI collaboration, judgment, and adaptability."

Trends 2026 post: "71% of leaders say AI is making technical skills harder to assess"; "over half (62%) of organizations still prohibit AI use in technical interviews"; chart values Live technical interviews US 79% / China 87%, Allow AI use US 38% / China 68%, Automated code tests US 63% / China 49%, Take-home projects US 45% / China 20%
date_and_recency: Highlights posted 11.04.2025 (image path suggests November 2025). Full PDF undated, titled 2025-2026; trends post dated 01.07.2026 (January 2026 by its position among later posts). Fieldwork window NOT stated in any source opened [uncertain]; the confidence comparison labels data as '2024' and '2025', implying 2025 fieldwork. Source of the 2024 baseline (presumably an earlier Karat survey) is not stated. No specific AI model versions referenced; an OpenAI VP quote says 'This year, we've moved from autocomplete to agents'. A newer 2026-2027 edition (Harris Poll, 157 leaders, U.S. and China, announced around October 2026) exists but only its preview was available.
key_claims: AI increases engineering productivity by an average of 34% (leaders' estimate).
AI is a multiplier, not an equaliser: strong engineers gain most; 73% say a strong engineer is worth at least 3x total compensation, 59% say weak engineers deliver net zero or negative value.
85% expect engineering headcount to stay flat or grow over three years; 68% name hiring new FTEs as the primary strategy for an AI-ready workforce.
Talent measurement is not keeping pace: 62% don't allow candidates to use AI in interviews, while leaders estimate over half of candidates use AI anyway.
Interviews that are not AI-enabled give 'useless' signal because most candidates use AI (Karat's assertion, not a measured validity result).
Producing a working solution no longer generates the same hiring signal; interviews must isolate underlying skills and assess AI readiness.
US hiring confidence is eroding and assessment is getting harder; 71% say AI makes technical skills harder to assess.
China is ahead on AI adoption and is almost twice as likely to allow AI in interviews, moving towards live interviews and away from take-homes and automated tests.
U.S. organisations using human-led interviews with AI allowed anticipate better outcomes (fewer coding errors, faster time to market, more features) than human-only or non-human assessment users.
headline_figures: 400 engineering leaders surveyed, including 300 SVPs and CXOs (highlights page: 'more than 300 SVPs, CTOs, and CIOs'), across U.S., India, China.
71%: 'leaders who say AI is making it harder to assess technical skills' (all leaders, 2025 survey).

62%: 'of leaders don't allow candidates to use AI in interviews' (PDF wording); trends post rewords it as '62% of organizations still prohibit AI use in technical interviews'. All three countries pooled.
'Over half' of candidates use AI despite instructions not to (leaders' estimate, not measured).
Hiring confidence: % of US leaders 'very confident that qualified candidates are the ones getting job offers' fell from 67% (2024) to 47% (2025).
Assessment difficulty: % of US leaders who say it is difficult to accurately assess skills needed to capitalize on new developments in AI rose from 19% (2024) to 36% (2025).

Allow AI in technical interviews: US 38%, China 68% (trends post chart). Live technical interviews: US 79%, China 87%. Automated code tests: US 63%, China 49%. Take-home projects: US 45%, China 20%. India values not given.
U.S. cohorts: Human + AI 33%, Human-only 45%, Non-human 22% of U.S. organisations.
Expect coding errors to decrease over 3 years: 63% (Human + AI) vs 45% (human-only) vs 21% (non-human).
Expect time to market to decrease: 49% (Human + AI) vs 31% (human-only) vs 20% (non-human).
Expect number of products/features released to increase: 76% (Human + AI) vs 57% (human-only) vs 48% (non-human).

30% rank updating technical assessments for AI as a top priority (p.4 text); the p.5 priority chart shows 25% Finserv / 33% Tech for 'Updating Technical assessments to assess for AI skills' and 22% / 27% for training interviewers, which does not cleanly match the '25% training interviewers' in the text.

34% average productivity increase from AI (leaders' estimate); 73% say strong engineer worth at least 3x total comp; 59% say weak engineers deliver net zero or negative value; 66% expect strong engineers' value to increase threefold over three years.
Top AI use today: code generation 83%, testing/QA/code review 61%, data/ML 56%, security 53%, agentic AI 54%.
sample_and_method: Survey of 400 engineering leaders (300 SVPs and CXOs) in the U.S., India and China. These are senior leaders, not individual software engineers or candidates. Per-country sample sizes, sampling frame, recruitment, survey mode, fieldwork dates, question wording, and weighting are not published in the PDF or the trends post. No Harris Poll attribution for this edition. Some headline numbers are U.S.-only (confidence, difficulty, cohort outcomes), others pooled. Outcome comparisons are respondents' expectations over the next three years, self-reported, cross-sectional, and not measured hiring outcomes.
what_is_measured: The survey measures leaders' opinions and practices: which assessment formats they use (live interviews, automated code tests, take-homes), whether AI is allowed, perceived difficulty of assessment, confidence that qualified candidates get offers, and expected business outcomes. As advocacy, it says interviews should measure underlying skills plus 'AI readiness', 'AI collaboration, judgment, and adaptability'. Desired skills listed: familiarity with agentic AI, using AI for coding, integrating third-party AI APIs, prompt engineering, evaluating and mitigating AI-related risks, with problem-solving, communication and product sense described as foundational constants.
ai_policy_in_interview: Reports on policy rather than setting one: 62% of leaders (pooled) don't allow AI in interviews; US 38% vs China 68% allow it. Karat advocates permitting AI in human-led live interviews.
scope_and_status: Not applicable (cross-sectional industry survey, not a rollout). Karat's own human-led AI-enabled interview product is mentioned on karat.com but its scope is not described in the report.
validity_evidence: None. No criterion-validity data (no correlations with on-the-job performance) for any format. The claim that AI-allowed human interviews are better rests on respondents' expected future outcomes (coding errors, time to market, feature count) split by the interview format their organisation uses. This is correlational, self-reported, and confounded by organisation type and AI maturity. The statement that non-AI interviews give 'useless' signal is asserted, not tested.
relevance_to_angle: Supports 'stop testing convergent coding': Karat says a working solution to a simple problem 'no longer generates the same hiring signal' and 71% of leaders say AI makes skills harder to assess. Supports 'working with an agent' and 'basic fluency': leaders want AI-native skills and Karat recommends interviews that allow AI. Partially supports 'communication and team fit' (communication named as a foundational skill) and 'design conversation' only loosely (judgment). Gives a useful tension: most organisations (62%) still ban AI in interviews while leaders think most candidates use it anyway, and US hiring confidence fell from 67% to 47%. Should be cited as a vendor survey with an interest in the conclusion.
limitations_stated: No limitations are stated in the PDF or the trends post. The report acknowledges a cultural confound only obliquely: 'To account for cultural differences in hiring, we looked at business outcomes from U.S. companies across three cohorts.'
counter_evidence: Vendor incentive: Karat sells the human-led, AI-enabled interview it recommends. Outcome differences are expectations, not measured results, and organisations already advanced in AI are likely both to allow AI in interviews and to expect bigger gains (reverse causation/confounding). 'Over half of candidates use AI' is a leader estimate. The 2024 baseline for confidence and difficulty has no stated source or comparable sample. Minor internal inconsistency: p.4 text says 25% prioritise training interviewers, while the p.5 chart shows 22% (Finserv) and 27% (Tech). Sample is senior leaders, not engineers or candidates. Later 2026-2027 edition uses a different, smaller sample (157, U.S. and China, Harris Poll), so figures should not be mixed across editions.
verification_status: Checked against primary sources actually opened (2025-2026 PDF and karat.com trends post): 400-leader sample; 71% harder to assess; 62% don't allow AI; over half of candidates estimated to use AI; US confidence 67% to 47%; US difficulty 19% to 36%; US/China format percentages (trends post); cohort shares and outcome expectations; 34%, 73%, 59%, 85%, 68%. Harris Poll role: confirmed only for the 2026-2027 edition via City A.M. (secondary press, 8 Oct 2026); NOT credited in the 2025-2026 report [uncertain whether Harris fielded the 2025-2026 survey, no source says so]. Fieldwork dates: not found [uncertain]. 2026-2027 sample of 157 vs Karat landing page's 150: secondary/preview only [uncertain].
